Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Robert, a sixty-year-old warehouse worker, had spent most of his adult life trying to keep the past at a distance, and for long stretches he had believed he was succeeding. He worked the night shift at a distribution center outside a small Midwestern town, stacking pallets and operating a forklift in the cavernous, fluorescent-lit space. The job required little conversation, and the constant hum of conveyor belts and the beep of reversing trucks filled his ears with a noise that pushed out thought. He drove home each morning just before sunrise, showered, and lay next to his partner, Linda, listening to the wind or the furnace until his body finally gave in to exhaustion. This rhythm had worked for years. What had begun to fail was his ability to stay inside it.

The event that had set this life in motion happened forty-two years ago, when Robert was an eighteen-year-old Marine in Vietnam. He still saw it in fragments, like a film reel that had been torn and spliced in the wrong order: the green-dark of the jungle, the crack of a single shot that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere, the sight of his squad leader, Sergeant Kowalski, crumpling to the ground with a hole in his throat. Robert had been the medic’s assistant, but the medic was already down, and the ten seconds that followed had erased every piece of training from his mind. He had frozen, kneeling in the mud, as the man next to him—Private First Class Delgado, who had been teasing him about a letter from home just minutes earlier—took a round to the chest and fell against him. Robert remembered the weight of Delgado’s body, the smell of blood and wet earth, the sounds of shouting and gunfire that seemed to go on forever. He remembered, too, the moment he realized he was still alive. The rest of the squad had taken cover and returned fire; the ambush ended as quickly as it had begun. Out of twelve men, four walked out. Robert was one of them.

For decades after returning home, Robert had not spoken about that day. He had learned to steer his mind away from it the way a driver avoids a pothole—automatically, without conscious thought. When a memory surfaced, usually at night or in a moment of silence, he would get up and find something to do: sweep the garage, organize his tools, fold laundry until his hands ached. Thinking about the event had become, over time, something he refused to do, as if the act of turning it over in his mind might make it more real, might invite it to stay. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that belief had settled into his bones so deeply that it felt like common sense. He scanned parking lots for men who moved too quickly. He sat with his back to the wall in restaurants. He had not been to a parade or a public fireworks display in over twenty years.

The guilt was worse than the fear. Robert had survived, and he was certain that he had done nothing to deserve it. He had frozen; he had not helped anyone. The faces of Delgado and Kowalski came to him when he least expected them—while he was standing in the grocery aisle, while he was waiting for the traffic light to change—and the feeling that rose in his chest was not just sadness but a kind of hot, physical guilt that made it hard to breathe. He could not find the words to describe what had happened, not even to Linda, who had asked him gently over the years. When he tried, the sentences would stall in his throat, and he would shake his head and say, “I can’t explain it.”

His avoidance began to take concrete, daily forms. He stopped wearing any shirt that buttoned down the front, because the khaki uniforms he had worn in the service were too similar. He gave away a grey work jacket that had the same cut as his field jacket. He drove a different route home from work every night, not because the direct way was close to the old VFW hall—he never went there anyway—but because he could not bear the thought of driving past the army recruiting station on Main Street. Its flag and its blue sign made his stomach clench. Over the months, the list of places he avoided grew: the post office, because it had a memorial plaque; the hardware store, because a veteran worked the register and might want to talk.

At the warehouse, the triggers were subtler but just as present. The smell of diesel from the forklifts could, on certain nights, turn into the smell of helicopter fuel, and Robert would find himself gripping the steering wheel so hard his knuckles went white. He avoided the far corner of the loading bay where a single bare bulb flickered, because the pattern of light and shadow reminded him of the jungle canopy. He had asked for a transfer to the quieter overnight shift, knowing it meant fewer people, less chance of being asked a question that might lead him toward the memory.

The consequences of these years of vigilance had accumulated. His relationship with Linda had become a careful choreography of unspoken rules. She knew not to touch him from behind, not to raise her voice, not to suggest they take a vacation to anywhere with woods or water. He had pulled away from her more than he realized; they slept in separate beds now because his nightmares made him thrash and cry out, and it was easier to be alone. He had stopped seeing his grandchildren, because the noise and unpredictability of small children sent his heart racing. He felt, most days, like a stranger wearing his own face. The identity loss was a hollow ache: he no longer knew who he was outside the shell of memories and routines.

What finally brought Robert to a clinic was not the guilt or the terror, but a small, practical failure. He had been assigned to train a new hire—a quiet young man in his twenties with a military-style haircut—and when the man had asked Robert where he had served, Robert had opened his mouth to say “I don’t want to talk about it,” and instead had begun to cry. He had walked off the floor and spent the rest of the shift sitting in the break room, staring at his hands. Linda had driven him to the appointment. He was afraid that talking about the event would make it worse, that the words would never come, and that he would be left with nothing but the guilt and the certainty that the world would never feel safe again. But he was also, for the first time in forty-two years, tired of running.

missing_explanations: The vignette describes guilt, fear, and physical reactions when remembering the event, but does not explicitly convey that remembering brings back the same terror experienced at the time of the trauma.
